newsitem.title: DENMARK: INTERVIEW - Bridge to lift Danish airport.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bridge to lift Danish airport.

text.p: A bridge linking Sweden and Denmark will boost Copenhagen international airport's position in Scandinavia, the airport's managing director Niels Boserup said.

The first link between Sweden and the European continent -- a tunnel, road and rail link due to be completed in late 2000 -- is expected to halve journey times between Sweden's third largest city, Malmo, and the Danish capital.
"Most of the business in Sweden is in an area south of Gothenburg and Stockholm," Boserup told Reuters in an interview.
"Copenhagen is already the airport for the southern part of Sweden. It's just a little more difficult to come here today than it will be in the future."
The bridge is expected to give the airport more passengers and cargo opportunities.
Currently there are only 1.6 million people in its catchment area and more than half of the airport's traffic is transit passengers.
The airport is also undergoing a 10 year investment programme worth about seven billion Danish crowns including a new pier with five gates and a second terminal.
The project will also connect the airport to a railway terminal.
"Trains will pass through the railway terminal from northern Sweden to the European continent. This will give us new opportunities passenger and cargo wise," Boserup said.
The airport has three runways, including two parallel ones that are 3,600 metres and 3,300 metres long. The third is only used in certain weather conditions.

The airport is rebuilding one of its three cargo terminals and Scandinavia Airline SAS is responsible for the installations. The new 24,000 square metre terminal will have an annual capacity of 350,000 tonnes cargo.
Passenger traffic through the airport, open 24 hours, rose 7.3 percent to 16.1 million people in 1996. It handled around 309,800 tonnes of cargo.
The airport, which was privatised in 1994, is an investor success story.
The government sold 25 percent of the shares in the company, whose full name is Copenhagen Airports A/S, for 310 crowns each.
In the spring of 1996 the government sold an additional 24 percent at a price of 510 crowns. The share closed at 680 crowns on February 20.
Market analysts say it's no secret the government will sell off the rest of its holding sometime.
"The market has been very satisfied with the performance of the share," Boserup said.
In 1995 the airport posted a profit of 247 million crowns net compared to 180 million crowns a year earlier. Its six-month profit in 1996 totalled 131 million crowns.
Boserup said the 1996 result would reflect higher costs.
"It's no secret that we've had a nice increase in traffic in 1996...so we have increased some of our costs," he said.
The airport plans to keep its airport charges unchanged until 1999 when European Union travellers will no longer be able to buy duty free goods, Boserup said.
"We will lose revenue and profit at that time," he said.
Boserup said the airport is also building a luggage sorting facility which will be safer -- it screens 100 percent of passenger baggage -- and faster.
"This will be in demand in Europe by the year 2000," he said.
